context_switch.note: One of the three that touch no Lua. Together with `exception` and `ipc_roundtrip` they are the control group: all three were identical to three decimals across taking the interpreter out of the kernel, which is the evidence that the kernel itself did not change.
context_switch.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

exception.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

gc_pause_max.note: The worst single collector step, measured in a process. 78199, against 78129 before gfx was added: +0.09%, which is the same effect as on serialize and far smaller, because a longer step is dominated by the 3000-object heap the benchmark builds rather than by a handful of library tables. Four runs spanned two ticks. Before that it was 77860, running inside the kernel with interrupts masked. Leaving EL1 cost the interpreter +0.3% and nothing else: a collector step costs the same at either privilege level. Interrupts are live in the window now, because a process cannot mask them, and for a pause metric that is more honest rather than less - a pause the user feels includes the tick that landed in it.
gc_pause_max.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

ipc_roundtrip.note: A minimal message: the floor of the IPC path, including the capability translation every delivery performs. Compare with `serialize`, which is what carrying a real Lua table costs on top - about forty-six times more.
ipc_roundtrip.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

serialize.note: Best of five processes within a run. Moved 1364.9 -> 1394.1, +2.2%, and the serialiser did not change: what changed is that every process now opens the gfx library. Measured rather than guessed - the same tree with the luaL_requiref for gfx commented out gives 1358.2, back inside the old range. The library table, the surface metatable and its methods are more objects on a 2 MB heap, so the collector paces differently through the measured loop. That is a property of this benchmark worth knowing before chasing it: **serialize is sensitive to what else is in the process**, not only to the serialiser, and it will drift again every time a library is added. If it moves and nothing in serialize.c or sys_user.c did, look at what was opened. Spread: four consecutive runs of the recorded image span 0.045% (1394.05 to 1394.68). Across builds made at different points the same source reached 1409.8, +1.1%, so roughly half the 2% tolerance is already spent on that. Before that it was 1037.6, when it measured serialize_pack/unpack called from C inside the kernel; it measures sys.pack/sys.unpack from a process now, which allocates a Lua string per round where the C version wrote into a struct message. Those two numbers are not comparable.
serialize.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0
